name: Enlightened absolutism
summary: Enlightened absolutism is the eighteenth-century idea that an absolute monarch should use reason, science and reform to improve his subjects' welfare while keeping all political power. The ruler is the first servant of the state, but subjects are not partners in government: everything for the people, nothing by the people.
scope: The eighteenth-century European strand of absolute monarchs influenced by the Enlightenment, in the defining sources' account (Britannica names Frederick II, Peter I, Catherine II, Maria Theresa, Joseph II and Leopold II): Frederick II's essay and 1752 Testament, Joseph II's patents and reforms, and Catherine II's Instruction as reported by scholarship. Excludes modern authoritarian modernizers.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: Joseph annexed Galicia in the First Partition of Poland, whose people were not consulted.

change-traditions-that-no-longer-suit.rationale: Joseph used reason and utilitarianism against meaningless traditions hindering the new social order.

citizens-assembly.rationale: Joseph held that subjects should have no voice in the political process, which excludes citizens' assemblies deciding public questions.

class-collaboration.rationale: Frederick says ruler and ruled are one body, and the Testament has the sovereign hold the balance between peasant and gentleman so they do not ruin each other.

clerical-rule.rationale: Joseph made secular priests an extension of state authority, and the doctrine puts the monarch at the head of the state.

conscription.rationale: Joseph's state aimed at access to each and every subject as taxpayer or soldier.

decide-locally.rationale: Joseph replaced administration by Estates and landlords with a central bureaucracy reaching every subject.

democracy-best.rationale: Joseph's maxim was everything for the people, nothing by the people, and he thought subjects should have no voice in politics.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: Britannica defines the doctrine as rule by absolute monarchs, which excludes a head of state chosen by popular election.

direct-votes.rationale: Joseph held that subjects should have no voice in the political process (everything for the people, nothing by the people).

dynastic-succession.rationale: Frederick came to the Prussian throne on his father's death.

elective-rulers.rationale: Britannica defines the doctrine as rule by absolute monarchs, which excludes an elected head of state.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: Britannica says these monarchs proposed no reforms that would undermine their sovereignty.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Joseph abolished the nobility's legal privileges and special courts, yet his Toleration Patent kept Catholic public worship alone and left non-Catholics second-class.

gradual-change.rationale: Joseph put his reforms into practice at precipitate speed and often too hastily.

head-commands-forces.rationale: Frederick calls the sovereign the foremost general of his country, and the Testament has all treaties and policy pass through his hands.

limit-population.rationale: The Nakaz said an increase in population was vitally needed to use Russia's natural wealth.

military-force-beyond-defence.rationale: Frederick invaded Silesia, and Joseph pursued wars for Bavaria and against the Ottomans to preserve Austria's rank as a great power.

military-superiority.rationale: Frederick built Prussia into the foremost military power in Europe.

minority-language-support.rationale: Joseph's wish to make German the sole language of administration ran against support for local languages.

minority-territorial-autonomy.rationale: Joseph centralised the Habsburg lands, provoking resistance in Hungary and the Netherlands.

nation-first.rationale: The Testament says the interest of the State is the only consideration that should decide a prince's counsel in choosing allies.

national-church-status.rationale: The Toleration Patent let the Catholic religion alone enjoy public practice of its faith, with others limited to private worship.

national-cultural-autonomy.rationale: Joseph's idea of the perfect state was a centralised nation state of unified citizens, not one with separate cultural self-government.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Joseph systematically extended welfare institutions such as Vienna's General Hospital, and reformed education, the church and the economy.

parliament-supreme.rationale: The Testament rejects deliberation in large assemblies, and the Nakaz kept the monarch supreme.

participatory-democracy.rationale: Joseph held that subjects should have no voice in the political process (everything for the people, nothing by the people).

party-controls-media.rationale: Joseph abolished censorship and tolerated public criticism even of himself.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Joseph abolished special courts and wanted officials to act strictly by the provisions of law, yet decreed a flood of reforms that many experienced as arbitrary.

restore-past-order.rationale: Joseph used reason and utilitarianism against meaningless traditions.

right-to-secede.rationale: Joseph's centralism overrode provincial administration and met open resistance in Hungary and the Netherlands without concession.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Frederick tells rulers to remember they are men like the least of their subjects and calls the sovereign merely the principal servant of the State.

separate-church-state.rationale: Joseph bound the church to the state: papal ordinances needed state approval and priests trained in state seminaries.

separated-powers.rationale: Frederick calls the sovereign the foremost judge, general, financier and minister of his country, and the Testament has him decide all branches himself.

single-common-good.rationale: The Testament says the wise sovereign pursues only the public interest and rejects advice from competing assemblies and ministers' interests; Frederick has the ruler act for the whole community.

single-official-language.rationale: Joseph wished to make German the sole language of administration and communication.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Frederick calls the sovereign the guardian of the law, accountable to the citizens for his stewardship, and the Nakaz held everyone subject to the same laws.

state-harmful.rationale: The Testament makes strengthening the State and its power the one aim of government, and calls the sovereign the first servant of the State.

strong-leader.rationale: Frederick's Testament says the sovereign must run the government himself, since a system can be the product of only one brain, and prefers this to conciliar bodies.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Joseph had papal ordinances approved by state committees and trained priests only in state seminaries.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Joseph tolerated public criticism even of his own person.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Catherine's Nakaz offered state subsidies and tariffs to help the growth of private industry.

taxation-theft.rationale: Joseph introduced a fixed tax rate and, for the first time, a property tax on aristocratic land.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Frederick took Silesia, and Joseph drove the annexation of Galicia and occupied Bukovina.

torture-always-illegal.rationale: Catherine's Nakaz called for abolishing torture in legal cases.

vote-delegation.rationale: Joseph held that subjects should have no voice in the political process, so no votes to delegate.

notes: Later pass 2026-11-23: Wikipedia-only sources replaced by Britannica, Frederick II's essay and 1752 Testament, Joseph II's Toleration Patent, Catherine's Nakaz as reported by EBSCO, and the World of the Habsburgs essays on Joseph II; earlier answers that rested on Wikipedia or inference are null or restated with a history entry. Themes searched: government, church, war and territory, language and centralisation, economy. No full text of the Nakaz was found online (searched the web and Wikisource/archive leads; only scholarly summaries). Catherine's and Charles III's own records are absent from the defining sources used, so those themes stay thin.
